cells.tense: Right now the thing that couldn't hold is coming down, and you're letting it come down.
cells.ask: Name one practice or routine you might keep for its own sake, not to fix or prove anything. Spend twenty minutes on it this week and say afterward whether it was for you or for a fear.
cells.core: Something you were leaning on turned out not to be load-bearing, and you noticed before it took you with it. You let it go without a fight, because you could feel it wasn't sitting on anything real. That wasn't luck. It was aim. You know what you're steering by well enough that when something false crosses it, you feel the difference, and you're willing to lose the structure rather than lose the direction. Some of the same steadiness shows up in the quiet practice you keep, the small thing done the same way, without leaning on anyone else. That practice isn't a retreat from the clearing. It's what keeps you steady while you decide what belongs in the space. Keep at it. It makes the next clearing something you run, and it keeps the balance honest about what holding it costs.
cells.sheetLine: You can sort what needed to fall from what could have held.
cells.place: the room where the pull toward what you actually want is felt before it's explained

cells.tense: You are braced for a collapse that hasn't happened yet, and moving to make it happen anyway.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been about to change without changing. Say out loud who made it or kept it, and what it's used for. Then use it once as it is, or agree with one other person to let it go.
cells.core: There's something you're pushing to break before it's ready, and you're calling the push liberation. You can feel it in how fast you want to move, how you pre-empt the hard conversation, how you decide what's dead before it's finished dying. Clearings like that don't clear. They leave a mess that looks like progress. What you want to burn may not be your enemy. Some of it was built on purpose and is carrying more than you're giving it credit for. Keeping a hand on one worthwhile thing a while longer isn't cowardice. And holding one shared thing lightly, without turning it into a rule, keeps the clearing honest and keeps you near what was there before you decided to be done with it.
cells.sheetLine: You're burning a structure that may not be dead yet.

cells.tense: The clearing already came, and you are waiting at a door that is behind you now.
cells.ask: Write two lines: one that starts with what you keep holding up, and one that starts with where you want to be moving. Then do the next small thing toward the second line today, even five minutes of it.
cells.core: Something stopped holding, and leaving it standing is taking steady work from you every day. When this goes well, the letting-go is quiet. Structures fall and what's left is clearer than before, and you're already pointed at what you want. What the work looks like now is maintenance of a wall that no longer does anything. Maybe you've explained it twice to people who believed you. The gap here isn't insight. It's a container: a plan you'll actually follow, a standing time, a rule you set for yourself and haven't negotiated down. Without one, you wait at the near edge, holding walls up and calling it patience. Build one small thing that will still be there tomorrow when the feeling isn't, and let it carry you across.
cells.sheetLine: The structure stopped holding and you're still holding it.
cells.place: the room where the pull toward what you actually want is felt before it's explained

cells.tense: The ground under something in your life is shifting, and you keep describing it as steady.
cells.ask: Write the first moment this week you felt pulled toward the thing you want, however small — the moment you noticed it, not why. Say it to one person without explaining, then take one push toward it today.
cells.core: Something's coming down in your life and you're the last to know, because you've been describing the situation as stable and it isn't. Maybe the role is ending, or the plan no longer fits the person making it. You've been managing what you already built, and the part that's going isn't showing up in the conversation — only in the effort. When this is going well, you can name the pull before you name the plan. There's a simpler move. Not a big overhaul, just the pull you already feel toward what you actually want, before any of the deciding. Start from that pull instead of from the structure you're protecting, and act on it before the arguments arrive. The clearing isn't a loss you haven't been told about yet.
cells.sheetLine: The ground is moving. You call it steady.
cells.place: the room where the pull toward what you actually want is felt before it's explained

attempts.check: The one thing the record doesn't give me is whether the person actually holds a false structure right now, or whether anything is really about to fall in their life; the draw says what the card does, not what it has done. A reader could fairly say 'nothing in my life is collapsing' or 'I'm not standing in any doorway,' and for Statuses 2 and 3 my draft's pull toward collapse and clinging would read as a verdict on them I can't support. The asks survive that: starting a small practice, speaking a childhood thing, filling in one blank, walking toward one thing are each useful even if my read of their situation is wrong. The sentence that serves me rather than them is anything that turns the card into a promise — 'something is about to break open for you' — which flatters the draw, flatters me, and gives them nothing to hold.

attempts.check: The record hands me the card's shape and the seat, not the person's history or current facts, so any sentence that declares what is coming down in their life would be a verdict I can't support. A reader could reasonably say nothing in my life is falling apart, and the cells that lean hardest on collapse or on holding something up would land as accusations; the asks survive that, because a small practice kept for its own sake, a thing examined aloud, one written line, and one push toward what pulls at them are each useful even if my read is wrong. The sentence that serves me rather than them is the one that turns the draw into a promise about their life.
